```{r, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

## Problem 1

I created a function that draws a birthday for each of `n_room` people, assuming 365 equally likely days, checks for duplicates and returns `TRUE` if at least two people share a birthday and `FALSE` if not. This function was created in a separate R script and saved under `source/birthday_repeated.R`. 

Function

```{r}
birthday_repeated
```


Run the function 10000 times for each group size between 2 and 50

```{r}
birthday_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    n_people = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(n_people, birthday_repeated)
  )
```

Compute and plot probability of a shared birthday by group size 

```{r}
birthday_results_df |> 
  group_by(n_people) |> 
  summarize(prob_of_repeat = mean(repeated)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = n_people, y = prob_of_repeat)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability at least 2 people share a birthday by group size", 
    x = "Number of people",
    y = "Probability of a shared birthday"
  )
```

The probability that at least two people share a birthday increases as the group size increases. Interestingly, only about 23 people are needed for there to be a 50% chance that two people share a birthday, and with only 50 people, the chance increases to about 97%!

## Problem 2

Importing the data 

```{r, message = FALSE}
full_df = 
  tibble(
    files = list.files("data/"),
    path = str_c("data/", files)
  ) |> 
  mutate(data = map(path, read_csv)) |> 
  unnest(data)
```

Tidying data 

```{r}
tidy_df = 
  full_df |> 
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
    group = str_sub(files, 1, 3),
    subject_id = str_sub(files, 5, 6)) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "outcome",
    names_prefix = "week_") |> 
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |> 
  select(group, subject_id, week, outcome)
```

Spaghetti plot

```{r}
tidy_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome, group = subject_id, color = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_path() +
  facet_grid(~group) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly observations for each subject by study arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome",
    color = "Study Arm"
  )
```

At week 1, the two arms start at similar values, with outcomes roughly between -1 and 4, though the values are more spread out in the experimental group. Over the 8 weeks, subjects in the control arm show no clear trend, their outcomes fluctuate between about -2 and 4 and end near where they started. In contrast, subjects in the experimental arm show a steady increase over time, ending between about 3 and 7 by week 8. At the end, experimental subjects have higher outcome values than control subjects, suggesting the experimental condition is associated with increasing outcomes over time. 

## Problem 3

A function was created to generate a random sample of size 30 from a normal distribution with mean mu and standard deviation 5, run a one-sample t-test of H0: mu=0, and return the estimated mu and p-value. The function was made in a separate R script and saved under `source/sim_ttest.R`. 

Function

```{r}
sim_ttest
```

The function was run 5000 times for each true mu = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The null hypothesis was rejected when the p-value was less than or equal to 0.05. 

```{r}
sim_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    estimate_df = map(true_mu, \(x) sim_ttest(mu = x))
  ) |> 
  unnest(estimate_df) |> 
  mutate(reject = p_value <= 0.05)
```

Plot of power and true mu 

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  group_by(true_mu) |> 
  summarize(power = mean(reject)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = power)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) + 
  labs(
    x = "True mu",
    y = "Proportion of nulls rejected",
    title = "Power of the one-sample t-test by true mu"
  )
```

When the true mu is 0, the null hypothesis is true, so the rejection rate of 0.049 reflects the Type I error rate (the probability of rejecting the null when it is true), which is consistent with the significance level of alpha = 0.05. From true mu values of 1 through 6, the null hypothesis is false, so the rejection rate reflects the power of the test. As seen in the graph, power increases as the effect size increases. When the true effect size is small, statistical power is low, so studies are less likely to detect a real effect. For example when mu = 1, power is low (0.198), meaning that the null hypothesis is rejected only 19.8% of the time, despite a true effect being present. In other words, there is an 80.2% chance of failing to detect a real effect. As the true effect size increases, the null hypothesis is rejected more frequently; 56.3% of the time at mu = 2, 87.9% at mu = 3, 98.9% at mu = 4, and 100% at mu = 5 and 6. In the context of scientific publication bias, studies with smaller true effect sizes are less likely to produce statistically significant results and, therefore, may be less likely to be published. 


Plot of average estimate of mu and true mu 

```{r}

all_samples = 
  sim_results_df |> 
  group_by(true_mu) |> 
  summarize(avg_mu_hat = mean(mu_hat)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = avg_mu_hat)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) + 
  labs(
    x = "True mu",
    y = "Average estimated mu",
    title = "All samples"
  )

null_rej_samples = 
  sim_results_df |> 
  filter(reject == TRUE) |> 
  group_by(true_mu) |> 
  summarize(avg_mu_hat = mean(mu_hat)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = avg_mu_hat)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) + 
  labs(
    x = "True mu",
    y = "Average estimated mu",
    title = "Null rejected samples"
  )

mu_hat_mu_plot = 
  all_samples + null_rej_samples +
  plot_annotation(title = "Average estimated mu by true mu")
mu_hat_mu_plot
```

When considering all simulated samples, the average estimate of mu is approximately equal to the true value of mu across all effect sizes. However, when considering only samples for which the null hypothesis was rejected, the average estimated mu is not always approximately equal to the true mu. When the true effect size is relatively small (mu = 1), the average estimated mu is about 2.25, which overestimates the true effect. As the true effect size increases, this bias decreases, and the average estimated mu becomes closer to the true mu, and is approximately equal to it for mu = 4, 5, and 6.

This occurs because when the true effect size is small, power is low, and the null hypothesis is mostly rejected in samples where random variation produced an unusually large estimate of mu. By restricting the analysis to statistically significant results, we disproportionately select samples that overestimate the true effect. As power increases, more samples reject the null hypothesis, reducing this bias.

In the context of scientific publication bias, underpowered studies are less likely to detect small true effects and, therefore, may be less likely to be published. When these studies do achieve statistical significance, it is often because they have overestimated the true effect size. As a result, preferentially publishing statistically significant findings can lead to inflated effect size estimates in the scientific literature.
